newsitem.title: SLOVAKIA: SLOVAK C.BANK STICKS TO AUSTERE MONETARY PLAN.
newsitem.headline: SLOVAK C.BANK STICKS TO AUSTERE MONETARY PLAN.

text.p: The National Bank of Slovakia (NBS) says it will maintain its current tight monetary policy, but some commercial banks are calling for a new approach to ease lending and support growth.
Several senior Slovak bankers have questioned whether the NBS should use the M2 measure of money supply as strictly as it does to determine monetary policy.
They say Slovakia's deeply under-capitalised economy needs further financial injections to continue reforms.

"In our opinion the M2 (rate) as a basic criterion for assesing monetary development should not be applied as strictly here as in fully developed market economies," Jan Gabriel, President of the largest commercial bank VUB, told the country's leading businessmen at a seminar last week.
The NBS has rejected calls to stop using the M2 benchmark, saying that if it did, it would be impossible to keep inflation within its target range.
"Our target is to keep the currency stable and maintain the so-far favourable development of inflation," Peter Sevcovic, head of the NBS Monetary policy departent, told Reuters.
"You can call it strict but it has has never been restrictive," Sevcovic said.
He added that the fact that M2 has so far always exceeded GDP growth was clear evidence of a non-restrictive policy.

Slovak inflation, still one of the lowest rates in post-communist Europe, rose 0.7 percent in October, putting prices 5.3 percent higher year-on-year. The official forecasts for next year's inflation foresee a rate of under six percent.
Gabriel said he expected M2 growth to be well under the NBS target of 11.6 percent this year.
He added, however, that credit expansion is likely to significantly exceed the NBS target of 7.2 percent year-on-year increase .
"There is no such direct connection (between these factors) as in market economies, since our economy is under-capitalised and needs money to progress in reforms" Gabriel said.
But Sevcovic disagrees:
"Of course there is a clear connection between credit expansion, money supply growth and inflation... We can not ease the policy and let inflation jump, for example, to 12 percent."
NBS vice-governor Marian Jusko last week said M2 growth in the first ten months of the year was at "around" 18 percent year-on-year, down from a 19 percent in September.
He said however that the central bank will not meet its full-year 11.6 percent target.

The overall volume of credits continued to rise in September by some 1.3 billion crowns ($48.69 million), putting the total volume at 355.4 billion as of September 30 - a 19.2 percent increase year-on-year.
Commercial banks also complain that recent unpopular central bank measures could hurt their competivenes against foreign institutions.

Last July, the NBS implemented a series of measures aimed at tightening the money supply and curbing inflation. The moves included hikes in the Lombard rate last-resort lending facility and of the minimum reserve requirements for banks.

Recently, the NBS adopted a new foreign exchange rule starting at the beginning of next year, allowing more liberal foreign credit position for Slovak entities, and further reducing domestic loan expansion.

Jozef Strasko, vice-president of the largest savings bank Slovenska Sporitelna, said the measures would make domestic financial sources more expensive by pushing interbank money rates, now at 12 to 14 percent, higher.

"High interest rates resulting from the measures may not only hurt competetivenes of Slovak banks, but will result in the slowdown of resources for restructuring of the economy," Strasko told the seminar.

Sevcovic said critics should instead adopt a positive attitude toward the NBS monetary targets, because they provide a stable currency and favourable inflation development, which will ensure investments will not be whittled away by inflation. -- Bratislava Newsroom, 42-7-563-3687
